/-!
# Erdős Problem 379

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/379](https://www.erdosproblems.com/379)
-/

namespace Erdos379

open Filter

noncomputable def S (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  sSup {s | ∀ k ∈ Finset.Ico 1 n, ∃ p, p.Prime ∧ p^s ∣n.choose k}

/--
Let $S(n)$ denote the largest integer such that, for all $1 ≤ k < n$, the binomial coefficient
$\binom{n}{k}$ is divisible by $p^S(n)$ for some prime $p$ (depending on $k$).Then
$\limsup S(n) = \infty$.

This was formalized in Lean by Tao.
-/

reformulations.difference: The Lean definition uses a natural-number supremum and assigns values even at n = 0, 1, where the source's largest-exponent description has an empty coefficient range. The limit superior is then taken in ℕ∞.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For n ≥ 2, the admissible exponent set is nonempty (it contains 0) and bounded: taking k = 1 gives a prime p with p^s ∣ n, hence s < p^s ≤ n. Its natural-number supremum is therefore its attained maximum. Downward closure gives s ≤ S n iff every coefficient with 1 ≤ k < n has a suitable prime-power divisor p^s. At n = 0, 1 the exponent set is unbounded, so Mathlib assigns S n = 0; these two initial values do not affect the limit superior. In the scratch file I proved the maximum characterization, invariance under shifting the sequence by two, and the equivalence of the theorem's proposition with: for every exponent s and cutoff N, there exists n ≥ max 2 N such that every 1 ≤ k < n admits a prime p with p^s ∣ n.choose k.
